newsitem.title: CHINA: China copper concentrate imports seen growing.
newsitem.headline: China copper concentrate imports seen growing.

text.p: China will import at least 150,000 tonnes of refined copper this year, depending on the price gap between Shanghai and London, but the spotlight will shine on concentrate imports, traders said on Tuesday.

China's refined copper imports in the first half of this year had been hit as London Metal Exchange (LME) prices soared above the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME), making imports into China far too expensive, industry sources said.
But the gap was closing and could soon bring China back into the market, they said.
"The arbitrage is becoming close to positive for the Chinese, and if it stays the same, then I see them coming back to buy," said one senior dealer.
On the Shanghai Metal Exchange, the most actively traded December 1997 contract ended on Tuesday at an intraday high of 20,460 yuan per tonne ($2,468), up 50 yuan.
LME copper staged a mini-rally early Tuesday from overnight 7-1/2 month lows of $2,135 a tonne, trading between $2,140 and $2,151 per tonne.
Traders multiply the LME cash price in dollars per tonne by 10 to get a rough equivalence in yuan per tonne, inclusive of import duties and taxes.
LME copper at $2,140 would be not too far from SME copper at 20,460 yuan.
Broker Macquarie Equities said in a Monday commentary that China would import 150,000 tonnes of copper this year to make up a shortfall, but that would not be enough to spark a price rally.
"I cannot tell the exact amount, but 150,000 tonnes may not be able to satisfy the Chinese market," a trader said.
Macquarie projected 1997 consumption at 1.35 million tonnes and production at 1.2 million tonnes, leaving the 150,000-tonne shortfall.
"I think the actual production figure should be lower than that at the refined metal stage. Refined production out of refiners is less than that," said another trader.
But huge Chinese copper smelters were gearing up for production and refined copper imports of 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes per year belonged to the past, traders agreed.
"The smelter expansions are coming under way, we've got Jinlong, by the end of the year, Daye, and then Jiangxi. They've all got the money, they're all building," another trader said.
As a result, concentrate imports were projected to grow significantly.

"Last year we had a big jump to over 800,000 tonnes of concentrate, this year they're already at 900,000 tonnes," the source said, noting he had heard estimates as high as one million tonnes of copper concentrate imports for 1997.
And the China Non-Ferrous Metals Import and Export Co (CNIEC) was sounding out long-term concentrate deals as well as investing in overseas copper mines, traders said.
According to an analysis by Shanghai's Colub, scrap imports in the first half were 277,000 tonnes, up 15.8 percent
China produced 596,500 tonnes of copper in the first seven months of this year, up 17.16 percent compared to the same period last year, the China Securities paper said earlier this month.
